posts.name: SellySel
posts.cooked:
Nadyssa:

What would you add to the game to cater to solo players?

How would a "solo player" design content for WoW?

I would expand upon the follower system to create a party of NPCs large enough to take on current raids so that raids could be soloed with a similar experience to the one people have today, but with all NPCs aside from the player. I would focus heavily on the fishing system, providing players with an artifact on the same level as the underlight angler and with fun new fishing themed abilities that show off their dedication to the craft, and extremely rare vendor fish that sell for big gold.

I’d bring back and expand the archaeology system, retroactively applying it to Shadowlands and to the Dragon Isles.

I’d double the number of quests, half of them being designed for post-cap play and finishing the advanced storylines would award a full set of max-level epic armor with bonuses related to questing/surviving/traversing the overworld.

I would also bring back MoP style daily quests and remove the daily quest limit as well as increasing the amount of quests you can hold in your quest log.

The NPC followers alone would open up an unfathomable amount of content for solo players, as this would allow everyone to solo legacy raids that still aren’t easy enough in WoW’s current state.

I would also introduce a ton of busywork achievements like “/tickle every gnome” or “/hug every dragon” or things of that nature like Northrend had when achievements first rolled out. Things to do while exploring the new zones and tangible rewards for completing them. Tabards, cosmetics, mounts, titles, pets, etc.

I’d double the number of quests, half of them being designed for post-cap play and finishing the advanced storylines would award a full set of max-level epic armor with bonuses related to questing/surviving/traversing the overworld.

I would also bring back MoP style daily quests and remove the daily quest limit as well as increasing the amount of quests you can hold in your quest log.

The NPC followers alone would open up an unfathomable amount of content for solo players, as this would allow everyone to solo legacy raids that still aren’t easy enough in WoW’s current state.

Seems once again many are not understanding just what an MMORPG really means so I have taken the liberty to once again post the definition for those who fail to comprehend.

What Does Massively Multiplayer Online Role-Playing Game (MMORPG) Mean?

A massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) is a video game that takes place in a persistent state world (PSW) with thousands, or even millions, of players developing their characters in a role-playing environment. The virtual world in which the game takes place is never static. Even when a player is logged off, events are occurring across the world that may impact the player when he or she logs in again.

Techopedia Explains Massively Multiplayer Online Role-Playing Game (MMORPG)

Unlike traditional console-based role-playing games where the overarching goal is to complete the game, MMORPGs depend on emergent game play based on the interactions of players and groups of players. Most MMORPGs still provide tasks and battles that get progressively harder, but the primary purpose of these is to help gamers build up their characters in terms of experience, abilities and wealth.

To keep the gaming experience evolving, MMORPGs allow players to form alliances, interact within the game, customize their avatars and even create some of the game content. Moreover, players who are not interested in entering dungeons and battles to build up their characters can still participate in the game by setting up shops in villages and cities to contribute to the authenticity of the game’s world.

MMORPGs also have their own economies, where players can use the virtual currency they’ve earned in battles to buy items. This virtual economy has crossed over into the real world in some areas. For example, MMORPG players have exchanged real currency for items and virtual currency. In some instances, players seeking to level-up their characters more quickly have employed farmers - gamers who play as another person’s character - who work to earn experience points for their employers while they are logged off.
